strengths: Establishes a rigorous and technically nontrivial measure-based framework connecting finite-prompt softmax attention to its infinite-prompt linear counterpart, with explicit non-asymptotic L2 concentration bounds for both outputs and gradients (Propositions 3.1, 3.4), going beyond prior moment-based concentration results (e.g., concurrent work of Bohbot et al.).

Extends the training-dynamics transfer argument to a general in-context learning setting (Theorem 4.3), showing that risk obtained by training on large finite prompts is asymptotically no worse than training on the infinite-prompt limit, via a clean Gronwall-based argument.

Applies the framework to in-context linear regression, obtaining the first convergence/Bayes-optimality guarantee for softmax attention under anisotropic Gaussian covariates (Theorem 5.2), improving on Chen et al. (2024), which is restricted to isotropic covariates and relies on more technical, architecture-specific arguments.

The proof strategy is comparatively compact and reusable (leveraging existing linear-attention analyses rather than re-deriving softmax dynamics from scratch), which is presented as a general toolkit applicable beyond the specific regression setting studied.

Numerical experiments (isotropic and anisotropic settings) qualitatively support the theoretical predictions—concentration of outputs/gradients, convergence of both models to Bayes risk, and shrinking distance between softmax and linear training trajectories as L grows.
Appendix provides detailed, careful proofs, including explicit constants and handling of subtle issues like autocorrelation between query and prompt tokens.
weaknesses: The central linearity mechanism (Lemma 2.1) relies crucially on the i.i.d. Gaussian (or centered Gaussian) assumption; the paper acknowledges but does not seriously grapple with how far this is from practical settings (non-Gaussian, non-i.i.d., positionally structured token distributions), limiting the practical relevance of the 'softmax behaves like linear attention' narrative implied by the title.

The concentration rates obtained (e.g., ln(L)/L^{c2/σ²}) are qualitative and can be very slow for large sub-Gaussian parameter σ, and no explicit convergence rates are given for the ICL linear regression result (Theorem 5.2), somewhat limiting the quantitative strength of the main application relative to concurrent/related work that does provide rates (Bohbot et al. 2025; Chen et al. 2024).

The framework is restricted to single-layer attention; extending to multi-layer transformers (which is where most of the interesting empirical phenomena around softmax vs linear attention arise) is left entirely to future work, restricting the paper's significance.

The empirical results are somewhat double-edged: linear attention consistently outperforms softmax attention at finite prompt length in the experiments, which, while consistent with the theory (both converge to Bayes-optimal as L→∞), makes the practical motivation (softmax attention's superior empirical performance, emphasized in the introduction) not obviously borne out by the experiments shown.

Some technical assumptions (Assumption 3.3, 4.2(iii)) involving bounded moment ratios are somewhat opaque regarding how restrictive they are outside the Gaussian ICL setting where they are explicitly verified; their generality is asserted more than demonstrated.

The theoretical guarantee in Theorem 4.3 is only in terms of asymptotic (t→∞) risk comparison and gives a comparatively weak, non-quantitative statement about parameter trajectories (Lemma E.1 only yields closeness along a specific slow schedule T(L)), rather than a full characterization of finite-time training dynamics equivalence.

strengths: The paper develops a technically careful measure-based framework that extends known infinite-prompt results (Vuckovic et al., Sander et al., Castin et al.) to non-asymptotic, finite-prompt concentration bounds for both the output and the gradient of softmax attention layers, which is a nontrivial technical contribution (L2 concentration vs. moment-only concentration in concurrent work by Bohbot et al.).

The extension from pointwise concentration to stability along the entire gradient-flow training trajectory (Theorem 4.3) is a meaningful step that allows transferring optimization results from linear attention to softmax attention.

The application to in-context linear regression (Theorem 5.2) generalizes existing softmax ICL convergence results (e.g., Chen et al. 2024, He et al. 2025) from isotropic to anisotropic covariates, with a comparatively simpler proof strategy leveraging the linear-attention analysis of Zhang et al. (2024).

The paper is transparent about related and concurrent work, clearly delineating its contribution relative to Bohbot et al. and Chen et al., and includes an extension to degenerate covariance matrices in the appendix.
Numerical experiments (including anisotropic covariate settings) are reasonably consistent with the theoretical claims and are described with sufficient implementation detail for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central thesis—that softmax attention becomes linear attention in the large-prompt regime—is essentially a restatement of the fact that softmax collapses to an affine map specifically for centered (sub-)Gaussian i.i.d. token distributions; this is a strong and somewhat self-selecting assumption under which the two mechanisms are already asymptotically identical by construction (Lemma 2.1), making the subsequent 'inheritance' of linear-attention theory for softmax less surprising than advertised.

The paper's own introduction motivates the work by noting that softmax attention empirically and theoretically should outperform linear attention, yet the paper's main results and experiments (Figure 2) show the opposite in the regime studied: linear attention achieves lower ICL risk than softmax at finite L, with the gap only closing as L→∞. The work therefore does not illuminate any advantage of softmax over linear attention, undermining its stated motivation.

No explicit convergence rates are given for the main training-dynamics results (Theorems 4.3 and 5.2); the authors explicitly state they do not pursue sharp rates, which limits the practical/quantitative usefulness of the 'large-prompt' claims (e.g., how large L must be in practice is not characterized).

Theorem 4.3 requires an a priori assumption that the infinite-prompt gradient-flow trajectory remains within a bounded ball; this assumption is non-trivial and must be separately verified case-by-case (as done via Zhang et al.'s results in Section 5), meaning the general theorem's applicability outside the specific linear-regression case is unclear.

The i.i.d., centered (sub-)Gaussian token assumption is quite restrictive and arguably unrealistic for real transformer inputs, which typically exhibit positional structure, autocorrelation, and non-Gaussian token distributions; the authors acknowledge this but do not provide evidence the framework extends beyond this setting.

The appendix reports that softmax training is more unstable than linear-attention training in some runs (requiring seed reruns), an observation that is interesting but not analyzed or connected back to the theory, leaving a gap between the stated equivalence and observed optimization behavior.

The overall contribution is largely a technical generalization (finite-prompt, anisotropic covariates, gradient concentration) of existing measure-based attention frameworks and existing linear-attention ICL dynamics results, rather than a new conceptual mechanism explaining softmax's distinct behavior.

strengths: Introduces a conceptually clean measure-based framework connecting finite-prompt softmax attention to its infinite-prompt (effectively linear, for Gaussian inputs) counterpart, providing a principled bridge between the widely-used linear-attention theory and the empirically dominant softmax attention.

Establishes non-asymptotic L2 concentration bounds for both the attention output and its gradients with respect to parameters (Propositions 3.1 and 3.4), going beyond prior work (e.g., concurrent Bohbot et al. 2025) that only controls moments of the output distribution; gradient concentration is essential for the subsequent training-dynamics results.

Extends the analysis along the entire training trajectory (Theorem 4.3) via a Gronwall-type argument, which is a nontrivial step beyond pointwise concentration and is the technical core enabling the application to in-context learning.

Applies the framework to in-context linear regression and obtains, to the authors' knowledge, the first convergence/Bayes-optimality guarantee for softmax attention under anisotropic Gaussian covariates (Theorem 5.2), improving on Chen et al. (2024) which required isotropic covariates, via a comparatively simple proof strategy leveraging the linear-attention results of Zhang et al. (2024).

The paper is transparent about limitations (no explicit convergence rates, comparison to concurrent/overlapping work, assumptions needed), and includes numerical experiments (including an anisotropic covariate setting) that qualitatively corroborate the theory.
Proofs are detailed and appear carefully constructed (extensive appendix with explicit constants and case-based arguments for heavy-tailed softmax weights).
weaknesses: All quantitative results rely on i.i.d. (sub-)Gaussian token assumptions, which is a significant departure from realistic prompts (tokens in real sequences are correlated, structured, and non-Gaussian); it is unclear how much of the theory would survive relaxing this assumption, and this is only briefly acknowledged in the conclusion as future work.

The concentration rates scale as L^{-c/σ^2} (and even worse polynomial/log factors for higher-order and gradient bounds), meaning that for the σ typically needed in interesting regimes (e.g., in the ICL application where σ_μ depends on ∥w∥ and can be unbounded/heavy-tailed), the effective sample complexity could be very large or the bounds vacuous; the paper does not discuss how tight or practically meaningful these exponents are.

The main in-context learning result (Theorem 5.2) provides no explicit convergence rate in L, is stated only as a qualitative ε-approximation, and essentially imports the heavy lifting (Bayes optimality characterization, limit values of U, V) directly from Zhang et al. (2024); the genuinely new technical content is the concentration/stability machinery rather than new optimization or statistical insight into the linear regression problem itself.

The result in Theorem 4.3 only yields guarantees on the asymptotic risk, not on convergence of the parameters themselves for a fixed finite L (the authors concede this explicitly), which somewhat limits the practical interpretability of the 'approximate training dynamics' claim.

The restriction to a single-layer attention model (no MLP, no multi-layer composition, no positional structure) limits applicability to understanding real transformers, and the experiments are correspondingly small-scale (d=5, toy synthetic ICL regression) without any validation on more realistic or larger architectures/tasks.

The paper's narrative sets up a motivating question ('why does softmax outperform linear attention empirically') but the actual theoretical conclusion is that the two become equivalent in the large-prompt limit under Gaussian inputs — the paper does not shed new light on softmax's empirical length-generalization/expressivity advantages over linear attention, somewhat under-delivering on the introduction's motivation.

Presentation is extremely dense and technical, with heavy reliance on sketches of proofs and delegation of nearly all substantive derivations to a lengthy appendix; the main text sometimes under-explains the practical implications and scope of the moment/regularity assumptions (e.g., Assumption 3.3, 4.2) for a general reader.
